questions.q: What two items does each node in a singly linked list store?
options: A value and a pointer to the next node.
A value and an absolute array index offset.
A value and pointers to both adjacent nodes.
questions.fact: A linked list is made of nodes; each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node.
why: Each singly linked node pairs payload data with a single next reference.
Linked list nodes do not use index offsets; they use pointer addresses.
Storing pointers to both neighbours defines a doubly linked list node.

questions.q: What does the next pointer of the final node in a singly linked list reference?
options: A pointer referencing back to the head node.
Null, indicating that no further nodes follow.
The total count of elements within the list.
questions.fact: The head pointer refers to the first node; the last node's next pointer is null.
why: Pointing back to head describes a circular list, not standard singly linked.
The terminal node points to null to signal the end of traversal.
Pointers store memory addresses, not element counters.

questions.q: How does the memory layout of a linked list differ from an array?
options: Nodes must be allocated in strictly contiguous memory blocks.
Nodes are stored in consecutive cache lines in sorted order.
Nodes need not be contiguous in memory.
questions.fact: Nodes need not be contiguous in memory.
why: Contiguous allocation is required by arrays, not linked lists.
Node locations are dynamically allocated without requiring cache continuity.
Each node is allocated independently on the heap and linked by pointers.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of inserting a new node at the head of a linked list?
options: O(1) constant time.
O(n) linear time.
O(log n) logarithmic time.
questions.fact: Insertion at the head is O(1).
why: Pointing new node to head and resetting head takes constant O(1) steps.
No memory shifting is needed because nodes are connected via pointers.
Head is tracked directly by a pointer, requiring no search.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of deleting the first node in a singly linked list?
options: O(n) because all remaining elements must shift left.
O(1) by updating head to point to head.next.
O(log n) because the list must be rebalanced.
questions.fact: Deletion at the head is O(1).
why: No shifting occurs; only the head pointer reference changes.
Advancing the head pointer to head.next immediately removes the first node.
Linked lists require no tree-like balancing during head removal.

questions.q: Why is inserting or deleting a node at a known middle position O(n) in general?
options: All nodes past that position must shift in physical memory.
The system must recompute hash buckets across the whole list.
You must walk from the head to find the preceding node.
questions.fact: Insertion or deletion at a known position requires walking to the node before it, so it is O(n) in general.
why: Nodes never shift physically; only pointer references are updated.
Linked lists do not use hash buckets to store or locate nodes.
Without direct indexing, finding the preceding node requires traversing from head.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of searching for a value in an unsorted singly linked list?
options: O(n) because nodes must be traversed sequentially from head.
O(log n) because binary search can halve pointer references.
O(1) because pointers provide instantaneous direct access to values.
questions.fact: Searching for a value is O(n).
why: Finding an element requires inspecting nodes one by one until matched.
Binary search cannot jump to middle nodes without random access indexing.
Pointers only allow sequential traversal, not direct access to arbitrary values.
